flawed_step: The first step fails: going from F_{X_n}(t) -> F_X(t) to any bound on P(|X_n - X| > eps). Convergence in distribution only involves the law of each X_n separately. P(|X_n - X| > eps) depends on how X_n and X are jointly distributed, which the CDFs do not determine.
counterexample: Let Omega = {H, T} with P(H) = P(T) = 1/2. Set X(H) = 1, X(T) = 0, and for all n set X_n(H) = 0, X_n(T) = 1 (so X_n = 1 - X). Both have CDF F(t) = 0 for t < 0, 1/2 for 0 <= t < 1, and 1 for t >= 1. So F_{X_n} = F_X everywhere, and X_n -> X in distribution. But |X_n - X| = 1 on every outcome, so P(|X_n - X| > 1/2) = 1 for all n, which does not tend to 0. Hence X_n does not converge to X in probability.
assessment_summary: The statement is false. Convergence in distribution depends only on the marginal laws, while convergence in probability depends on the joint law. In the counterexample X is Bernoulli(1/2) and X_n = 1 - X: the two have the same distribution, but |X_n - X| = 1 always. The implication does hold when X is a constant.
